summary: The hook-mode recall gate (strongOnly) lives here and has two independent bypasses that decide whether a note is injected: a term is 'rare' if its notebook df <= ceil(N/10), OR strongTerms >= HOOK_CONVERGE_MIN(4). VERIFIED 2026-07-27 by replaying .metrics/inject-log.jsonl: the entire suppression branch is skipped when notes.length < HOOK_FLOOR_MIN_NOTES(30), so a repo under 30 notes has NO gate at all (coldstart's own 28-note notebook: 0 suppressions in 218 decisions, 64% of them single-term). The shape rule at the strongOnly eligibility check trusts nameRaw = title + aliases MERGED as an 'authored' channel, but aliases are written as free-text prose, so ordinary English words in them (stop, compact, resume, memory, and the tokenizer artifact 'didn') become weight-3 name-channel tokens: 126 of 142 plain-English single-term carriers matched alias-only. Channel trustworthiness measured in that replay is monotonic with how much authoring went in - anchor(paths/symbols) > title > aliases > body - and body is the WORST (any common word lands in a long note body once by chance, so the heaviest grazes all sit at bodyTf=1).

summary: The hook-mode recall gate (strongOnly) has two bypasses deciding injection: a term is 'rare' if notebook df <= ceil(N/10), OR strongTerms >= HOOK_CONVERGE_MIN(4); the whole suppression branch is SKIPPED when notes.length < HOOK_FLOOR_MIN_NOTES(30). MEASURED 2026-07-27 against a 60-item blind-labelled sample of .metrics/inject-log.jsonl: today's gate injects 55/60 at 27% precision (63% of injections are grazes). CORRECTION to an earlier claim in this note - aliases are NOT sloppy prose: median 3 words across both the coldstart and arches notebooks, and the long ones are well-formed symptom phrases exactly as the capture guidance asks. The defect is in CONSUMPTION, not authoring: haystacksFor does [title, ...aliases].join(' '), so a multi-word symptom phrase is flattened into independent single-word weight-3 match surfaces (93% of alias tokens are plain English, because a well-formed sentence necessarily contains ordinary words). Three candidate fixes were replayed against the blind labels and ALL converge on a ~37-38% precision ceiling while each costs 20-30pp of recall: no-lone-alias-carrier (38%/75% recall), removing the <30 exemption (25%/50% - WORSE than doing nothing), and treating each alias as a phrase unit needing 2-token coverage (37%/63%). Do not ship a matcher-side patch on this evidence. Separate real bug found: wordHit is a strict \b regex with no stemming, so the query 'fire' does not match the note title 'how notebook capture fires'.

summary: Hook-mode recall (strongOnly) decides injection through: per-term eligibility (minority df + a shape rule), then a suppression gate that a hit escapes if any term is 'rare' (df <= ceil(N/10)), OR strongTerms >= HOOK_CONVERGE_MIN(4), OR (added 2026-07-29) the hit has convergence; the whole suppression branch is still SKIPPED under HOOK_FLOOR_MIN_NOTES(30). CHANGED 2026-07-29, all four verified by replaying 238 logged queries from .metrics/inject-log.jsonl: (1) wordHit is now stem-tolerant (light Porter step-1 + an 'e' allowance, so fires/fired/firing reach 'fire') — and the ORDER TRAP that makes it work: the presence check earlier in the term loop is SUBSTRING containment and runs BEFORE the shape gate, so a term whose surface form is absent was dropped before wordHit ran; stemming alone was a no-op until that check got a hook-mode-only stem escape. (2) convergence now also bypasses the suppression gate — it was computed, carried onto the hit and used by shouldImplantTop, but never consulted there. (3) resolveTermToSymbolFiles is no longer gated on isCodeShaped at its call site: isCodeShaped is a SPELLING test (digits/underscore/hyphen/interior caps), NOT a 'matches the codebase' test, so it rejected `keeper` though src/keeper.ts exists and the channel fired on 1 of 236 queries; the shape asymmetry moved INSIDE the resolver, where an English word must equal a whole identifier token and only code-shaped terms may match a fragment — plain substring there is a lottery (164 terms resolved but only 8 were real symbol names: `but` matched ensureGitattri[but]es, `see` matched par[seE]xperience). (4) hits now carry `carriers` (term:channel, c=converged) so the inject-log records which words did the work. NET on the 238-query replay: injections 147 -> 182, convergence 1 -> 27, 4 losses all genuine grazes; roughly half the gains are relevant and the rest are a NEW graze class — a common word that is also a symbol name (`status` in an HTTP 403 body now pulls the coldstart-status note). No guard was added for it, deliberately: every filter measured here loses more than it saves. STILL TRUE from the 2026-07-27 blind-labelled n=60 study: aliases are NOT sloppy (median 3 words); the defect is in CONSUMPTION (haystacksFor flattens title+aliases into single-word weight-3 surfaces); and the three fixes replayed then — no-lone-alias-carrier, removing the <30 exemption, alias-as-phrase-unit — all hit a ~37-38% precision ceiling at 20-30pp recall cost and remain REFUTED. Also refuted by measurement 2026-07-29: gating the rarity bypass on isCodeShaped kills 122 of 144 injections here and gains 0.

summary: Hook-mode (strongOnly) scoring: prose terms reach ONLY the name channel (title+aliases) via wordHit; the anchor channel is code-shaped-only; body coverage alone is never a hit; hookNameNorm divides the name channel by note size relative to corpus average. SHIPPED 2026-07-30 (PR #114): HOOK_MIN_CARRIERS drops any hook hit carried by fewer than 2 terms UNLESS the note's path was named OR one carrier is code-shaped OR one converged on a declared symbol in the note's own anchor (tracked by the hardEvidence flag set beside carriers.push). CORRECTS this note's earlier claim that plain '>=2 carriers' was the rule to ship: single-carrier hits are not one population — plain prose with no convergence is 3 good / 53 junk (5% precise), code-shaped is 4/2 (67%), converged is 7/8 (47%), so the defect is one ORDINARY WORD, not one term. Blunt >=2 keeps only 68% of good hits; the shipped split keeps 86% while removing 47% of junk (precision 31% -> 47%, volume 438 -> 280 over 563 logged prompts). The filter sits INSIDE the scoring loop, so a dropped top hit lets the runner-up rank — a variant that instead suppressed the whole page was built, measured, and REVERTED as overfitted to a small single-subject notebook. excludeIds is applied LAST, after trimmed.slice(0,max), so dedup shrinks the page and never pulls up a note the cap already rejected; it is hook-supplied state, so the engine itself stays stateless.

summary: Ranking contract (changed 2026-07-30): tiers rank CLAIMS, not evidence age. Only `inactive` (every anchored file gone from this branch) and `status !== active` (withdrawn) demote a note below score; anchor drift does not. Staleness WAS a hard tier and lexicographic order made it absolute — one changed byte in one cited file sank a note below every fresh one at any score, burying the top-scoring note on 50% of 249 logged prompts (median 1.4x, displaced to ranks 7-21). Flow notes were the systematic casualty: they anchor N files so they go stale ~Nx faster (100% of flows vs 30% of file notes) and reached a 3-slot page on 2% of queries against ~30% by chance; now 44%. Partial-`missing` is deliberately NOT a tier either — it is the same any-anchor binary rule one lane over and would re-sink the same multi-anchor notes. Freshness now only labels, via `[evidence changed: ...]` in gistLines. Hook-mode scoring reads name+anchor ONLY: term eligibility requires a plain word to whole-word-match the authored name channel, so body length cannot qualify a term (measured: flows and file notes carry the same ~2.5 terms in hook mode; in tool mode flows cover 44% more terms but BM25 length normalization claws it back to +13%). The anchor channel is the one unnormalized volume advantage — a 5-anchor flow gets ~20% more score on equal carriers.

MEASURED AND REJECTED 2026-07-30 — natural-language TITLES for file notes: fold.ts already accepts them (path is only a fallback), but they are not a new signal. Title and aliases are ONE channel, and hookNameNorm divides that channel by its own token count, so the name channel is ZERO-SUM: adding a title to a note taxes every alias it already has. Backfilling all 34 file notes with plain-English verb-phrase titles was actively harmful (+15 injections, -8, and the new ones grazed on generic verbs like `build` sitting in the highest-weight channel); retrying with 10 distinctive noun-phrase titles was a no-op (+1, -2, both losses on the notes with the longest alias lists). Do not re-propose titles as a recall fix — the lever is FEWER alias words, not more.

summary: The notebook search engine, in two modes that behave very differently — and the mode is chosen by `strongOnly`, NOT by any option named `hook`. THIS IS A MEASUREMENT TRAP: KbSearchOptions has no `hook` field, so calling kbSearch(root, q, {hook:true}) silently runs TOOL mode (loose BM25 scoring, no graze gate), and the convergence channel is off unless you also pass notesIndex (cli.ts:183 sets `strongOnly: flags.hook` and loads loadKbNotesIndex — copy that, do not improvise). Verified 2026-07-31 by replaying the logged corpus both ways: 274 queries injected in the accidental tool-mode run vs 182 in real hook mode, with 816 hits vs 396 — every conclusion drawn from the wrong-mode run was void, including a merged-PR-grade claim about alias capping. If you are replaying inject-log/miss-log to evaluate a ranking change, assert your run is hook mode before you believe any number. Second thing verified this session: single-carrier hits DO get through HOOK_MIN_CARRIERS via the hardEvidence escape at line 516 (`converged || isCodeShaped`), and in this repo's corpus 68 of 83 single-carrier hits arrived by convergence — one ordinary word matching a declared symbol admits a note with no other evidence. Hand-labelling those showed the good ones ride rare terms (descent, quiet, kbView) and the junk ones ride common ones (status, write, command, mcp), so convergence needs a rarity check rather than a blanket block.

summary: The notebook search engine, in two modes chosen by `strongOnly` — NOT by any option named `hook`. MEASUREMENT TRAP: KbSearchOptions has no `hook` field, so kbSearch(root,q,{hook:true}) silently runs TOOL mode and the convergence channel is off unless you also pass notesIndex. Copy cli.ts:183 (`strongOnly: flags.hook` + loadKbNotesIndex); do not improvise. Verified by replaying the logged corpus both ways: 274 injecting queries / 816 hits in the accidental tool-mode run vs 182 / 396 in real hook mode — every conclusion from the wrong-mode run was void. Assert your run is hook mode before believing any replay number. HOW A HIT IS ADMITTED IN HOOK MODE (all three gates are near line 550, read them together): (1) HOOK_MIN_CARRIERS — two carriers, unless hardEvidence; (2) hardEvidence — set by a code-shaped term OR by convergence, and as of 2026-07-31 convergence ALSO requires the term to be rare (df <= rareMax), because a term merely being a declared symbol is not evidence when the symbol is `name`/`status`/`write`/`command`; 68 of this repo's 83 single-carrier hits arrived that way and hand-labelling split them cleanly on rarity; (3) NAME_ONLY_MIN_DENSITY — a hit whose every carrier is name-only needs two query terms inside ONE authored string (title or a single alias), applied only to notes that HAVE anchors, since a lesson note has none by construction and would otherwise be permanently unfireable. Known surviving hole: rarity is note-level df, so a homonym that is rare inside a small notebook still gets through — `status` sits in two notes here, so 'server returned status 403' still reaches src/status.ts. That is the wrong-DOMAIN cause and needs a different mechanism. Gating additionally on how many anchored files declare the symbol was tried and changed nothing on this corpus, so it was removed rather than shipped on speculation.

summary: The notebook search engine, in two modes chosen by `strongOnly` — NOT by any option named `hook`. MEASUREMENT TRAP: KbSearchOptions has no `hook` field, so kbSearch(root,q,{hook:true}) silently runs TOOL mode and the convergence channel is off unless you also pass notesIndex; copy cli.ts:183 (`strongOnly: flags.hook` + loadKbNotesIndex). Verified by replaying the logged corpus both ways: 274 injecting queries / 816 hits in the accidental tool-mode run vs 182 / 396 in real hook mode. HOW A HIT IS ADMITTED IN HOOK MODE (three gates near line 550, read together): (1) HOOK_MIN_CARRIERS — two carriers unless hardEvidence; (2) hardEvidence — a code-shaped term, OR convergence that is ALSO rare (df <= rareMax), since a term merely being a declared symbol is not evidence when the symbol is `name`/`status`/`write`; (3) NAME_ONLY_MIN_DENSITY — a hit whose every carrier is name-only needs two query terms inside ONE authored string, applied only to notes that HAVE anchors. That gate is NARROWER than it reads: a term also present in the note's summary/body is a body carrier, so it only fires when every matched term lives in title/aliases and nowhere else. DENSITY, NOT BREADTH — measured 2026-08-01 on 279 logged prompts in real hook mode: the gate drops 38 hits (~34 junk by hand-label), and an escape hatch for terms touching 3+ different alias groups re-admits 8 of them, 7 junk (`one`+`arms` reached trigger.mjs across six of its aliases). Alias breadth measures the note's vocabulary volume, not the match, so it is anti-correlated with quality — do not re-propose it. Known holes, both measured and deliberately left: a code-shaped term matching an alias via the squash form gets no density credit (wordHit splits on alnum, so `max_files` never equals a token of `max files`) — 1 hit on this corpus, junk; and a carrier that converged on a COMMON symbol skips the density gate entirely, which a stricter variant changed by zero hits.

summary: The notebook search engine, in two modes chosen by `strongOnly` (hook = precision-first admission gates; tool = BM25, no gates). Measured 2026-08-02 on 34 real agent queries against a 115-note notebook: tool-mode P@1 is 52% and the note the agent actually used sits at rank 2 in 10 of 23 cases. Two ranking defects behind that. (1) TYPE INVERSION: file notes are 81% of a notebook and 35% of rank-1 slots but only 17% of what agents cite; flow notes are 19% of supply and 65% of demand. A file note's title is a bare path while the query is a sentence. Forcing file notes below flow notes lifts P@1 52%->61%, but breaks queries that name a symbol, so the real rule must be conditional on the query containing a path/symbol token. (2) LANE-2 PHANTOM EVIDENCE at the `!inAnchor && !opts.strongOnly && termFiles.get(t)?.size` branch: in tool mode a term with zero presence in a note's own text still scores a full anchor-channel occurrence if it matches any symbol declared in a file that note anchors. arches/settings.py wins rank 1 for 'bulk data manager sort order tiles' with 5 of 6 carriers phantom. Hook mode disables this deliberately. Hard-gating it (requiring text confirmation) costs recall and is the wrong fix; down-weight instead.

summary: The notebook search engine, in two modes chosen by strongOnly (hook = precision-first admission gates; tool = BM25, no gates). HOOK-MODE RARITY (separate from the tool-mode lane-2 phantom evidence already noted here): df at L430 is document frequency across name+anchor+body COMBINED, so a term that is a widely-declared anchor symbol inflates its own df even when it never appears in prose. Two different thresholds use it: eligibility (`minority`, L510, df*2<=notes.length, ~50%) drops a term from scoring entirely if it fails; hardEvidence (`rareMax=ceil(N/10)`, L178/516/543) requires the stricter top-10% band before a symbol-convergence hit can admit a note alone, UNLESS the term is code-shaped (isCodeShaped, L278) which bypasses rarity outright. Risk: in a domain-concentrated codebase a real entity name (e.g. an ecommerce Order/Shipment declared as an anchor symbol on many file notes) can fail hardEvidence's rarity band via the SAME mechanism that correctly suppresses generic filler (run/status/write) -- notebook-wide df does not distinguish 'generic English' from 'domain-central but frequent'. Untested on this repo's own notebook (too small/self-referential); needs a real domain-heavy notebook (e.g. ARCHES) to size.
